stories.headline: Atlanta Hawks offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: With the Trae Young era in the past, how do the Hawks move forward? We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season.
stories.body:
The Atlanta Hawks are entering the first full season of the post-Trae Young era with heightened expectations. After dealing their star point guard away last season, they've also moved on from 2024 No. 1 pick Zaccharie Risacher and brought in role players Aaron Wiggins, Ryan Nembhard and Luguentz Dort to strengthen their depth. CJ McCollum, the hero of their two first-round playoff wins against the eventual champion New York Knicks, is back as well, with Kingston Flemings, the No. 8 pick in the 2026 draft, backing him up.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Hawks coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason. The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall. Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Zach Kram's offseason grade: A-

Depending on how coach Quin Snyder structures his rotation, the Hawks might not have added a single starter this offseason -- although they did well to re-sign CJ McCollum to a solid one-year deal -- so their short-term ceiling still relies on Jalen Johnson's development into a star.

They made fairly dramatic upgrades to their bench, however, to meaningfully raise their floor. They acquired Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Devin Carter in salary dump trades, as well as Ryan Nembhard to help stabilize the backcourt. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: Zaccharie Risacher was the biggest draft miss in years.

Evidently, Onsi Saleh, who was promoted to general manager last summer, had seen enough. The 46-win Hawks were better with Risacher off the court last season, and he seemingly lacks the burst, playmaking and takeover mentality to develop into a lead scoring option. While the 2024 draft was regarded as weak at the time, Risacher ranks 20th in his class by career win shares and has been outperformed by Stephon Castle and several other lottery picks, plus a few players drafted 20-plus spots after him, including Baylor Scheierman, Kyle Filipowski and Oso Ighodaro.

Risacher's value dropped to the point that the Hawks didn't recoup a first-round pick in their three-team trade with the Mavericks and Oklahoma City Thunder. Instead, they added guards Luguentz Dort and Ryan Nembhard as they continue to build out their depth in the post-Trae Young era. -- Golliver

The big question: Can Johnson take the next step and win a playoff series?
Johnson averaged 22.5 points, 10.3 rebounds and 7.9 assists last season when Atlanta pivoted from Young and handed over the keys to the franchise to the versatile 6-8 forward. Johnson made the All-Star team and helped Atlanta become the only team to take two games off the eventual champion Knicks. But they also blew a 2-1 lead by losing three straight, including suffering an embarrassing 140-89 loss in Game 6 to New York. That should have left a lasting bitter taste for the Hawks all offseason and motivate Johnson to show he can take another step forward and lead the Hawks to a playoff series victory as their main star. -- Youngmisuk

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 17
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Hawks' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

The Hawks' starting unit last year was the second-best unit in the league (at least 400 possessions together). The Hornets' was best and they broke it up; Atlanta is sticking with it (unless rumors of Dort starting are true). The Hawks were 19-21 and ninth in the East before acquiring a key part of that lineup in CJ McCollum. They were 27-15 the rest of the way and beat the Knicks twice in the playoffs. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Post-free agency Power Rankings: Hawks are No. 14
Marks: Hawks could have cap space in 2027
Grades for every trade, including Dort, Wiggins

Biggest X factor
C Onyeka Okongwu

The Hawks are bursting with perimeter depth after trading for Dort and Wiggins, drafting Flemings and re-signing McCollum to a one-year deal. But Jock Landale -- a fine backup but not remotely a quality NBA starter -- provides the only depth at center, which means the starter, Okongwu, has a great deal of responsibility resting on his shoulders.

Okongwu developed into a capable stretch big last season, making 38% of his 5.2 3-point attempts per game. But he still needs to gain more scoring efficiency overall, as well as serve as a strong backline defender behind Dort, Dyson Daniels and the rest of Atlanta's perimeter stoppers. -- Kram

Bet to make ahead of the season: To make playoffs (-145), to win Southeast Division (+320)

The Hawks traded Trae Young on Jan. 7, and after that trade finished with a 29-15 regular-season record that was the seventhbest in the NBA in that span. The Hawks then went up 2-1 on the eventual champion Knicks in the playoffs, the only team to win two games against New York during the playoffs. The Hawks return their core that finished the season, led by budding star Jalen Johnson, and supplemented that with two contributors from the Oklahoma City Thunder championship team (Dort and Wiggins) as well as a lottery pick in Flemings. They seem poised to continue and improve upon their strong finish in the upcoming campaign. -- Andre' Snellings

Sept. 3: Thursday morning's news to know
By Todd Zola

Today's nine-game docket features three matinees and six evening affairs. Action gets underway at 12:30 p.m. ET with the Pittsburgh Pirates hosting the San Francisco Giants in the rubber game of a three-game set.

Yesterday afternoon, Adley Rutschman missed his third straight game. The Boston Red Sox indicated that the recently acquired catcher is dealing with a hyperextended elbow, which could be an issue for the rest of the season. The club was noncommittal regarding another possible IL stint. Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper will handle the catching chores while Rutschman is sidelined.
Ceddanne Rafaela left yesterday's game early with a tight quad, though the Red Sox noted the removal was precautionary. The club was down seven runs at the time. The Seattle Mariners went on to win 8-3 to win the series. Rafaela is day-to-day in advance of the Red Sox heading to Camden Yards for a four-game set with the Baltimore Orioles.
Joshua Baez didn't start last night's game for the St. Louis Cardinals, but he did enter the game as a pinch-hitter, then stayed in to play left field. He helped key the team's 8-6, 10-inning win over the Los Angeles Dodgers. Baez was hit by a pitch on Tuesday night, so when Baez wasn't in Wednesday's starting lineup, there was concern.
The Dodgers placed Eric Lauer on the 15-day IL due to an inflamed left elbow. He had struggled on Tuesday, surrendering seven runs in only three frames. With Roki Sasaki and Lauer sidelined, Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski are candidates to join the rotation.

Be sure to check out the latest fantasy lineup advice as well as the MLB betting tips for Thursday.

Sept. 2: Wednesday's news to know

By Todd Zola

The first Wednesday slate of September features six matinees, beginning at 12:40 p.m. ET with the Cincinnati Reds entertaining the San Diego Padres in the rubber game of a three-game series. Nine evening affairs follow, featuring the leading Cy Young contenders from each league. Dylan Cease and Cam Schlittler are neck and neck in the American League, while the honor is Jacob Misiorowski's to lose in the National League.

The Tampa Bay Rays are expected to activate Griffin Jax from the 15-day IL as they go for a sweep over the New York Mets. He's been out since early August due to a sore elbow. The right-hander completed just one rehab start, throwing 42 pitches, so he's likely to be on a pitch count.
The Chicago White Sox are also getting reinforcement for their rotation, with Davis Martin set to come off the IL to start tonight's road tilt against the Houston Astros. After finishing May with a 2.00 ERA and an 0.99 WHIP, Martin has struggled with a 7.06 ERA and a 1.73 WHIP.
Assuming that James Wood isn't sore after playing in a rehab game last night, he's expected to return to the Washington Nationals lineup. He's been sidelined since early August as a result of a strained left oblique. Wood has now completed two rehab games in advance of his pending activation.
Riley Greene returned to the Detroit Tigers lineup last night. The outfielder had been out since mid-August due to a strained hamstring. Greene returns to a team that is playing out the string. They hung in the AL wild-card race for a bit after the trade deadline, but the Tigers have won only three of their last 17 contests, dropping them to seven games out of the last spot (and behind five other still-chasing teams).
The Los Angeles Dodgers backstop situation enjoyed a boost with both Will Smith and Dalton Rushing returning from the IL. Rushing is expected to spend the rest of the season as a reserve, while Smith shares catching duties with Hunter Feduccia. The club hopes that Smith can return to form by playoff time, although he was on pace for the worst season of his career prior to suffering his neck injury.

stories.headline: Fenerbahce: Mason Greenwood, Matteo Guendouzi subject of UEFA investigation
stories.summary: Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.
stories.body:
Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.

Fenerbahce's 2-1 win away at Lyon in a Champions League qualifier ended amid ugly scenes involving Greenwood and Guendouzi who both previously played for Marseille, the rivals of Lyon.

Guendouzi raised his middle finger to Lyon fans during the warmup and after the game and shouted "Allez l'OM" ("Go Marseille"), also grabbing his crotch, in wild post-match scenes. He said Lyon fans insulted his family before and during the game.

A post-match scuffle included someone wearing Lyon club colours confronting Guendouzi, before several players became involved in an incident in the tunnel.

It was unclear if UEFA's disciplinary judges will sanction the players before Fenerbahce opens the Champions League main phase next Thursday, hosting Roma. Fenerbahce's second game is at Aston Villa on Oct. 14.

A Fenerbahce statement read: "Following the UEFA Champions League playoff round second leg match, UEFA has initiated disciplinary proceedings against our players Matteo Guendouzi and Mason Greenwood, as well as against our club.

"Our club will present the necessary defences before the relevant UEFA bodies in order to protect the rights and interests of our players and Fenerbahce during this process.

"The necessary information, documents and defences regarding the process will be submitted to UEFA, and developments are being closely monitored by our club. We hereby inform the public."

Fenerbahce qualified for the Champions League for the first time since 2008-09 at Lyon's expense after a 3-2 aggregate win.

Former Manchester United striker Greenwood joined the Turkish club this summer from Marseille in a €39 million ($44.5m) deal.

stories.headline: Andoni Iraola: Bradley Barcola could make Liverpool debut against Ipswich
stories.summary: Andoni Iraola has said new signing Bradley Barcola could make his Liverpool debut in Friday's Premier League clash with Ipswich Town.
stories.body:
Andoni Iraola has said new signing Bradley Barcola could make his Liverpool debut in Friday's Premier League clash with Ipswich Town.

The forward brought to an end a summer-long saga when he completed his move to Anfield from Paris Saint-Germain on Monday, joining for an initial £106 million ($143m) plus a potential £17m ($23m) in add-ons.

His last competitive appearance came for France in their 6-4 defeat to England on July 18 however, after joining up with his new teammates this week, the 24-year-old is likely to feature in the matchday squad at Portman Road.

"We are very happy with Bradley," Iraola said in his pre-match news conference. "It was our priority, let's say, to sign a very, very good player in that position. He has come also with the right mentality. I liked from him that he wanted Liverpool a lot.

"He just wanted to come here and I think that is a good first sign. Being the player that he is and the things that he has won recently, he has come with the willingness to help us. I am very happy with him and he trained well with us. If everything goes well in training today, he will definitely be available for tomorrow's game."

Asked whether Barcola could start Friday's game, Iraola added: "It's a good question. I see him in a good place, he has trained with us in three trainings. It is true he hasn't had minutes in preseason but he has been training normal with the group and then it's a decision we have to make. I think he is in a good place but we have to consider he hasn't had the minutes in the preseason games."

Barcola was Liverpool's fourth signing of the summer, following the arrivals of Jérémy Jacquet, Víctor Muñoz and loan signing Ronald Araújo. While the Reds ended the window with the highest net spend of any Premier League club, they have failed to strengthen in a number of key areas -- and Iraola hinted he would have liked more reinforcements.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over 8 seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would set new standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Cale Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers like Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win back in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the pinata while he's under contract.

We can tsk tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player that logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL that believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's gotta sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether or not the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman that'll be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He's got a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the Expected Goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the Expected Goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this mega-deal.

Winner: Player Empowerment
As I wrote back in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players that take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.summary: Formula 1 action is back in full swing and next up on the calendar is Monza, also known as the "Temple of Speed."
stories.body:
Formula 1 action is back in full swing and next up on the calendar is Monza, also known as the "Temple of Speed."

McLaren's Lando Norris sealed back-to-back victories after winning the Dutch Grand Prix to kick off the second half of the season last time out.

Kimi Antonelli is leading the championship by 59 points and following behind is his teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton both in second.

The Italian youngster will be hit with a grid penalty at his home race for taking a new engine.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know about the Italian Grand Prix.

- Max vs 100: F1 superstar Verstappen to race drivers in karting event - live on Disney+

- Franco Colapinto signs new contract to stay at Alpine for 2027

- Red Bull still won't be granted engine upgrade opportunities, rivals Mercedes and Ferrari will

Italian Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Friday, September 4

Practice One: 11.30 a.m. - 12.30 p.m.

Practice Two: 3 p.m. - 4 p.m.

Saturday, September 5

Practice Three: 11.30 a.m. - 12.30 p.m.

Qualifying: 3 p.m. - 4 p.m.

Sunday, September 6

Italian Grand Prix: 2 p.m.

How to watch

Sky Sports has exclusive F1 rights again in 2026 in the U.K., with every session live on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Italian Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Autodromo Nazionale Monza

The "Temple of Speed" is known for its long straights and heavy braking zones, and is the fastest track in Formula 1 history by overall average lap speed.

It's another classic circuit that has been on the calendar since 1950, only missing one year of racing in 1980 due to upgrading the track infrastructure.

It has one of the best podiums in the world as the famous Ferrari-loving tifosi flood onto the track after the race is finished. It's always a sight to be seen, especially if you are a Ferrari driver or an Italian driver.

Italian Grand Prix

Circuit: Autodromo Nazionale Monza; Monza, Italy

Previous winners
2016: Nico Rosberg, Mercedes

2017: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2018: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2019: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2020: Pierre Gasly, AlphaTauri

2021: Daniel Ricciardo, McLaren

2022: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2023: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2024: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2025: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

Other key stats

First F1 race: 1950

Lap record: 1:18.792, Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Laps: 53 laps of 5.8km. Total distance 306km

Most poles: Lewis Hamilton has seven at this circuit (2009, 2012, 2014-2017, 2020). Other pole sitters from the grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022), Max Verstappen (2021 and 2025), Carlos Sainz (2023) and Lando Norris (2024).

Most wins: Lewis Hamilton (2012, 2014-2015, 2017-2018) and Michael Schumacher (1996, 1998, 2000, 2003, 2006) are tied on five wins each. Other winners from the current grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Pierre Gasly (2020), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2024) and Max Verstappen (2022, 2023 and 2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the Italian Grand Prix is forecast to be sunny all weekend with light winds, with highs of 32°C on Sunday.

What happened last year?

Max Verstappen set the pace with the fastest lap in F1 history after getting pole position in Monza.

The Dutchman set a time of 1:18.792 breaking Hamilton's record from 2020.

It was McLaren's Norris who was on provisional pole before Verstappen beat him to the line in the closing stages.

Verstappen then went on to win the race in commanding fashion, but there were some team orders taking place at McLaren.

Norris was running in second for the majority of the race, but after a slow pit-stop, the team asked Oscar Piastri to move aside and let him teammate back through for second place.

At the time, Piastri was leading the championship from Norris by 31 points.

Who will win this year?

The biggest news entering the weekend will be Antonelli's engine penalty that will hamper his opportunity to score maximum points during the race.

He leads the championship after winning six races, but title fights can change quickly, as we saw during the backend of the 2025 season.

McLaren's upgrades have certainly been working, but team boss Andrea Stella said that Monza will be the true benchmark in terms of its performance and progress.

Ferrari will be hungry to get a home win with either of its drivers, but Monza will typically suit those strong in straight line speed and high-speed corners, such as Mercedes.

Monza could be one of the best opportunities to close the gap in the title race and take advantage of Antonelli not being a threat at the front of the pack.

stories.headline: 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup: Team USA analysis, rankings, rosters
stories.summary: Sixteen nations will compete in the World Cup in Berlin starting Friday. Team USA and France are front-runners.
stories.body:
The WNBA season is paused for the next couple of weeks, but there's plenty of women's basketball being played. The 2026 FIBA World Cup begins Friday and will run through Sept. 13 in Berlin, Germany. The tournament might not be as prominent as the Olympics -- to fans, at least -- but it is one of two major international competitions, with this year's event featuring 16 teams from North America, Europe, Asia and Africa.

The United States is, per usual, stacked, though the reigning champions suffered a blow when it was announced Monday that four-time WNBA MVP A'ja Wilson and five-time All-Star Kelsey Plum are unable to participate in the tournament due to health reasons. But those losses don't alter the task at hand: bringing home a fifth consecutive World Cup gold and 12th overall.

The U.S. women's national team plays its group phase opener Friday against China. The USA faces Italy on Sunday and then Czechia on Monday. If the U.S. women win their group, they move on to the quarterfinals on Sept. 10, with the semifinals set for Sept. 12 and the championship and third-place games on Sept. 13.

There are plenty of other familiar faces in Berlin, too, with dozens of current and former WNBA players representing other countries, from Australia to Türkiye.

ESPN's World Cup guide gets you set with everything you need to know before the games tip. Not every roster has been finalized yet, but we list current WNBA players on each squad, along with their stats for this current WNBA season.

Jump to:

AUS | BEL | CHN | CZE | FRA | GER

HUN | ITA | JPN | KOR | MLI | NGR

PUR | ESP | TUR | USA | GROUPS

1. United States
Current WNBA players:

F/C Aliyah Boston, Indiana Fever (16.9 PPG, 8.3 RPG, 1.3 BPG)

G Paige Bueckers, Dallas Wings (20.5 PPG, 5.9 APG, 4.1 RPG)

G Sonia Citron, Washington Mystics (16.8 PPG, 4.3 APG, 1.2 SPG)

G Caitlin Clark, Indiana Fever (22.5 PPG, 8.4 APG, 3.9 RPG)

F Napheesa Collier, Minnesota Lynx (18.0 PPG, 7.3 RPG, 1.4 SPG)

F/G Kahleah Copper, Phoenix Mercury (21.3 PPG, 3.6 RPG, 1.9 APG)

G Chelsea Gray, Las Vegas Aces (12.0 PPG, 6.8 APG, 1.4 SPG)

G Rhyne Howard, Atlanta Dream (18.3 PPG, 3.6 APG, 2.3 SPG)

F Kiki Iriafen, Washington Mystics (15.3 PPG, 9.4 RPG, 0.7 SPG)

F Angel Reese, Atlanta Dream (16.1 PPG, 12.4 RPG, 1.8 SPG)

F Breanna Stewart, New York Liberty (20.4 PPG, 8.1 RPG, 1.4 BPG)

G Jackie Young, Las Vegas Aces (18.9 PPG, 6.6 APG, 4.4 RPG)

Outlook: The U.S. women's national basketball team is home to one of the most dominant dynasties in all of sports, winning eight consecutive Olympic gold medals and four straight World Cups. The program has lost just one game at a major international competition since 1994 -- the semifinals of the 2006 World Championship (later renamed World Cup) against Russia, where the Americans won bronze. Team USA has since won 30 consecutive World Cup games.

That is the legacy newly minted national team director Sue Bird, senior national team coach Kara Lawson and this young U.S. squad -- a group with seven players under 27 -- bring to Berlin. Fans have long anticipated seeing the likes of Clark, Bueckers and Reese compete against international competition as part of the senior national team. They got a taste of that at the World Cup qualifying tournament, where the USA went 5-0 and won by an average margin of 42 points.

But between the grueling schedule, heighted competition and pressure of representing the USA, the World Cup will be a much greater challenge. USA Basketball's youth movement will be tested even more so with Wilson, the reigning World Cup and Olympics MVP, and Plum no longer available. But they still have a core of experienced veterans in Stewart, Gray, Collier, Young and Copper, who know what it takes to win gold. -- Alexa Philippou

2. France
Current WNBA players:

G Pauline Astier, New York Liberty (9.2 PPG, 2.5 RPG, 3.4 APG)

F Valeriane Ayayi, Phoenix Mercury (6.3 PPG, 2.7 RPG, 1.3 APG)

G Marine Johannes, New York Liberty (8.5 PPG, 2.1 RPG, 2.4 APG)

G Leila Lacan, Connecticut Sun (11.6 PPG, 1.9 RPG, 4.6 APG)

G Carla Leite, Portland Fire (15.9 PPG, 2.1 RPG, 6.3 APG)

C Dominique Malonga, Seattle Storm (17.0 PPG, 9.0 RPG, 1.5 BPG)

F Janelle Salaun, Golden State Valkyries (12.9 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 1.2 APG)

G Gabby Williams, Golden State Valkyries (14.3 PPG, 3.3 RPG, 2.2 APG)

Other notable players: C Marieme Badiane

Outlook: France, seen as the top threat to Team USA, might have its most talented roster ever with eight active WNBA players, four of whom will be headed to the playoffs. France has been building as an international power for the last several years. The French nearly toppled Team USA in the Olympic final in Paris in 2024, falling 67-66 behind former UConn star Williams' 19 points. France also took Olympic silver in 2012 and bronze in 2021.

France's only medal in the World Cup was a bronze in 1953, the first year of the event, but they are expected to have a podium finish this year. Malonga, the 2025 No. 2 WNBA draft pick who dunked in the All-Star Game in July, might look to do that in the World Cup. -- Michael Voepel

3. Spain

Current WNBA players:

G Elena Buenavida, Minnesota Lynx (developmental player)

C Raquel Carrera, New York Liberty (1.4 PPG, 1.1 RPG, 0.3 APG)

F Maria Conde, Toronto Tempo (8.9 PPG, 4.6 RPG, 2.6 APG)

C Megan DiLeo, Portland Fire (13.2 PPG, 4.2 RPG, 0.6 BPG)

C Awa Fam, Seattle Storm (10.3 PPG, 5.7 RPG, 0.9 SPG)

G Alicia Florez, Washington Mystics (3.3 PPG, 2.0 APG, 0.6 SPG)

Other notable players: G Iyana Martin, G Maite Cazorla

Outlook: Spain has had a relatively quiet output on the international stage in recent years. They medaled at the World Cup in 2010, 2014 and 2018 and took silver at the 2016 Olympics -- but then didn't even qualify for the previous World Cup in 2022 or the podium in Paris.

Coming off a silver-medal finish at last year's EuroBasket -- and more recently giving the USA its closest game of March's qualifying tournament -- Spain could be poised for a big showing in Berlin. The team is led by veteran Alba Torrens, the only player with World Cup experience, and has a naturalized star in DiLeo, who was a top-five scorer at the 2024 Olympics. Carrera has seen limited time with the Liberty but has been much more productive with her national team. What might be most anticipated, though, is the emergence of Spain's young tandem of 20-year-old stars in Storm rookie Fam and Martin, the Fire's draft-and-stash first-round selection. -- Philippou

4. Belgium

Current WNBA players:

G Julie Allemand, Toronto Tempo (6.3 PPG, 3.1 RPG, 5.6 APG)

C Kyara Linskens, Phoenix Mercury (3.0 PPG, 2.4 RPG, 0.7 BPG)

F Antonia Delaere, Minnesota Lynx (2.9 PPG, 0.7 RPG, 1.1 APG)

Other notable players: F Emma Meesseman, G Julie Vanloo, F Bethy Mununga

Outlook: Belgium should be one of the powers of Group C, along with Australia. The Cats are coached by longtime former WNBA coach Mike Thibault, who won a title with the Washington Mystics in 2019 when Meesseman was WNBA Finals MVP. Meesseman has played nine seasons in the WNBA, most recently last year when she spent 20 games (including the playoffs) with the New York Liberty. Vanloo played briefly (five games) with the Liberty this season. This is Allemand's fourth season in the WNBA, and she has been a starter for the expansion Tempo. This is Belgium's third World Cup appearance; they finished fourth in 2018 and fifth in 2022. Belgium has not medaled at the Olympics but had its best finish in Paris in 2024, falling in the bronze medal game. -- Voepel

5. Germany

Projected WNBA players:

F Frieda Buhner, Portland Fire (6.3 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 0.7 APG)

G Leonie Fiebich, New York Liberty (10.2 PPG, 3.0 RPG, 1.1 SPG)

C Luisa Geiselsoder, Portland Fire (4.5 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 1.3 APG)

F Nyara Sabally, Toronto Tempo (12.3 PPG, 5.3 RPG, 0.9 BPG)

* Roster not yet finalized

Outlook: Just like in the Olympics, a World Cup host faces a mixture of pressure and opportunity, and it's no different for Germany in what is just its second time participating in the event (and first since 1998). Unfortunately the Germans will be without the services of star Satou Sabally, who has stepped away from basketball while recovering from the effects of her second concussion in eight months, and it's unclear how healthy her sister, Nyara, will be. For the Germans to earn their first podium finish at a major international competition, they will need a huge tournament from Fiebich, who has been showcasing her value with the Liberty upon returning from injury. But also expect the likes of Buhner and Geiselsoder to play even bigger roles than they do stateside in Portland. Germany is coached by Olaf Lange, current Tempo associate head coach and Sandy Brondello's husband. -- Philippou

6. China

Projected WNBA players:

C Han Xu, New York Liberty (6.4 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 0.7 BPG)

* Roster is not yet finalized

Outlook: China should be the toughest challenger to Team USA in Group D, and the two play in the event opener for both. But the team was dealt a blow Wednesday when 6-foot-7 Dallas Wings center Li Yueru said on social media she will not be competing in Berlin because her passport was lost in the mail.

The United States and China faced off twice at the 2022 World Cup, with the U.S. women winning by 14 in group play and by 22 in the gold medal match. That result was still a win for the Chinese, though, as it marked the first time since 1994 that they earned a medal at a major international competition (both were silvers).

China faltered at the 2024 Olympics, finishing in ninth, before punching its ticket to the World Cup at this spring's qualifying tournament in Wuhan. This roster has some new faces compared to that '22 squad, headlined by the 7-foot-2, 19-year-old Zhang Ziyu. But she's not the only player who could pose some trouble for the USA, as the more experienced Han Xu (6-11) brings additional height. -- Philippou

7. Australia

Current WNBA players:

F Chloe Bibby, Minnesota Lynx (2.3 PPG, 0.7 RPG, 0.7 BPG)

G Isobel Borlase, Atlanta Dream (4.6 PPG, 1.5 RPG, 1.0 APG)

C Ezi Magbegor, Seattle Storm (6.9 PPG, 4.0 RPG, 1.2 BPG)

G Jade Melbourne, Seattle Storm (9.5 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 3.9 APG)

F Alanna Smith, Dallas Wings (6.0 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 1.0 APG)

G Miela Sowah, Golden State Valkyries (0.3 PPG, 0.8 RPG)

F Stephanie Talbot, Las Vegas Aces (3.5 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 1.0 APG)

Other notable players: F Alex Fowler, G Alex Wilson

Outlook: Phoenix Mercury guard Sami Whitcomb, captain of the Australian team, had to withdraw from the World Cup last week because of an ongoing knee injury. It's a big blow to the Opals regarding leadership and scoring. And it's heartbreaking for Whitcomb, who is 38. She was replaced by Sowah, 26. Sandy Brondello, who won WNBA titles with the Mercury (2014) and New York Liberty (2024) and is now with the Toronto Tempo, is Australia's coach.

The Opals began to emerge as an international power in women's basketball in the 1980s and won their first World Cup medal with a bronze in 1998. Their highlight was 2006, when they defeated Russia for the gold medal after the Russians had upset the United States in the semifinals. They also won bronze in 2002, 2014 and 2022, and took silver in 2018. Australia's six total World Cup medals puts them third on the all-time medal chart. The Aussies also have six Olympic medals: three silvers and three bronzes. -- Voepel

8. Italy

Current WNBA players:

G Costanza Verona, Dallas Wings (developmental player)

F Cecilia Zandalasini, Golden State Valkyries (8.8 PPG, 2.2 RPG, 1.8 APG)

Other notable players: F Lorela Cubaj

Outlook: Italy is enjoying a resurgence on the FIBA stage: Last year the team won its first EuroBasket medal since 1995 by beating France for the bronze medal, and now this World Cup marks the country's first appearance at a major international competition since the 1996 Olympics. Led by Zandalasini, the Italians lost 93-59 to the United States at the qualifying tournament in Puerto Rico, but went 4-1 overall at the event, including upsetting Spain the day after playing the U.S. women (and it's largely the same squad Italy has in Berlin). Italy has a difficult path ahead, though, having to face both the USA and China, the 2022 World Cup silver medalist, in the group phase. -- Philippou

9. Nigeria

Projected WNBA players:

F Amy Okonkwo, Portland Fire (4.3 PPG, 1.0 RPG, 0.3 APG)

* Roster not yet finalized

Outlook: This is the fourth time Nigeria has qualified for the World Cup, although it withdrew in 2022. That was much to the chagrin of the Nigerian players and FIBA. It was a decision by the Nigerian government, which opted in May 2022 to withdraw all its basketball teams from international competition while it restructured the sport's governance. Nigeria earned its World Cup berth this time by winning the AfroBasket 2025 championship. The team still played in the World Cup qualifying tournament in France in March, but lost three of five games. Nigeria's best finish in the World Cup is eighth, in 2018. The team's best Olympic finish is also eighth, in 2024. -- Voepel

10. Japan

Current WNBA players:

G Mai Yamamoto, Las Vegas Aces (5.8 PPG, 1.8 APG, 0.8 SPG)

Other notable players: G Rui Machida, G Kokoro Tanaka, C Ramu Tokashiki

Outlook: American basketball fans have come to enjoy Japan's entertaining style of play in recent years, particularly since squaring off against the USA in the 2020 Olympic gold medal game. Japan is known for speed, movement and 3-point shooting, which means the team can beat anyone if it gets hot -- and can lose to anyone if it can't hit shots. Lack of size is often an Achilles' heel -- just one player, Tokashiki, is listed over 6-foot.

Still, look out for the likes of Yamamoto, a midseason addition to the Aces, as well as Golden State draft pick Tanaka to make a splash on the perimeter. After the high of clinching silver at the Tokyo Olympics, Japan finished ninth at the 2022 World Cup, 12th at the Paris Olympics and almost didn't qualify for Berlin. Corey Gaines, the coach of the 2009 Phoenix Mercury championship squad, took over as head coach in early 2025. The pressure is on for them to find their form going into 2030, when they will host the next World Cup. -- Philippou

11. Hungary

Projected WNBA players:

F Dorka Juhász, Minnesota Lynx (3.8 PPG, 2.6 RPG, 1.2 APG)

* Roster not yet finalized

Outlook: While France is a big favorite in Group B, Hungary might make some waves behind Juhász. That especially could be the case with JiSu Park out for Korea and Nigeria looking kind of inconsistent entering the tournament. Hungary is making its sixth appearance in the World Cup but first since 1998. The team's best finish was fifth in 1957. -- Voepel

12. Korea

Current WNBA players:

G Jihyun Park, Los Angeles Sparks (2.2 PPG, 1.0 RPG, 0.5 APG)

Outlook: Korea is typically known as a strong outside shooting team. The team will need to rely even more on its guards with center JiSu Park, who played three seasons with the Las Vegas Aces, out due to an ankle injury. Korea is making its 18th World Cup appearance; it has played in every tournament except the first two in 1953 and 1957. Korea has won two silver medals, in 1967 and 1979. The team also has finished fourth three times, most recently in 2002. Korea has one medal in Olympic play, a silver in 1984. -- Voepel

13. Türkiye

Projected WNBA players:

G/F Kennedy Burke, Connecticut Sun (8.8 PPG, 3.2 RPG, 1.4 APG)

* Roster not yet finalized

Outlook: Türkiye will learn a lot about its chances from its opener vs. Belgium. This is Türkiye's third appearance in the World Cup; the team was fourth in 2014, when it hosted the event, and 10th in 2018. In her seventh year in the WNBA, Burke is having a career-best season. -- Voepel

14. Mali

Projected WNBA players:

G Aicha Coulibaly, Chicago Sky (4.8 PPG, 2.8 RPG, 0.7 SPG)

F Sika Kone, Atlanta Dream (1.7 PPG, 1.0 RPG)

* Roster not yet finalized

Outlook: Mali will make its third World Cup appearance, where it hopes to improve on an 11th-place finish in 2022. The program established itself as the second-best team out of Africa behind Nigeria, which beat Mali in the 2025 AfroBasket final. But Mali followed that up with a promising showing during the qualifying tournament in March, beating Czechia and narrowly losing to Brazil to clinch a spot in Berlin. Maimouna Haidara was the team's leading scorer in Wuhan, followed by the Dream's Kone; they'll need those two to dazzle to cause some upsets in Group A. -- Philippou

15. Czechia

Current WNBA players:

G Eliska Joklova, Minnesota Lynx (1.7 PPG, 1.1 APG, 1.0 RPG)

Outlook: Czechia is back at the World Cup after last appearing in the event in 2014; in 2010, it was the host nation and earned silver. The team's return this year has already been met with some concern. Czechia eked into the World Cup after a tepid qualifying tournament and has had some bad injury luck to two key players: Emma Cechova tore her ACL three games into her season with the Minnesota Lynx after a promising start, while Julia Reisingerova is also unavailable due to injury. On top of that, Czechia has to face the United States, China and a surging Italy squad in group play. It'll need sensational outings from the likes of Lynx rookie Joklova (née Hamzova), Veronika Vorackova and Petra Holesinska to keep up. -- Philippou

16. Puerto Rico

Current WNBA players: None

Other notable players: G Arella Guirantes, C Imani McGee-Stafford

Outlook: Host Puerto Rico was fourth in the qualifying tournament won by the United States in March in San Juan. A tough group awaits in Berlin, especially having to face Australia and Belgium. This is Puerto Rico's third appearance in the World Cup, having finished 16th in 2018 and eighth in 2022. Guirantes played two seasons in the WNBA, most recently in 2023. McGee-Stafford played four seasons in the league, most recently in 2019. Puerto Rico has competed twice in the Olympics. -- Voepel

Groups

Sixteen teams will compete in the FIBA World Cup in Berlin, Germany, with 36 games being played over 10 days from Sept. 4 to Sept. 13. The first-place team in each group advances to the quarterfinals; the second- and third-place teams will qualify for a single-game elimination format to determine the rest of the quarterfinalists.

stories.headline: State of Origin: Darius Boyd replaces Billy Slater as Queensland coach
stories.summary: Queensland's search for a new State of Origin coach is over, with Maroons legend Darius Boyd to take over in 2027 after signing a two-year deal.
stories.body:
Former Queensland star Darius Boyd will lean on the legacy and advice of former mentors Mal Meninga and Wayne Bennett after being appointed as the new Maroons coach.

The Queensland Rugby League confirmed on Thursday that Boyd would take up the position in 2027 on a two-year deal after Billy Slater stepped down from the role after five years.

Boyd, who won NRL premierships with Brisbane and St George Illawarra in a 337-game career, played 28 State of Origin matches for the Maroons and was a key figure in the dynasty under Meninga.

As a coach Boyd has led the Queensland U19 team to wins in back-to-back interstate clashes after being a member of the coaching staff at the Broncos under Kevin Walters for three seasons.

Boyd, who also played 23 Tests for Australia, said he was "extremely honoured" to be entrusted with coaching Queensland's State of Origin team.

"It's a privileged position and I'm very grateful for the opportunity," Boyd said.

"I understand the responsibility that comes with the role as well. My job is to build on the legacy created by the many great Queensland players and coaches who have come before us."

Boyd, who said Slater had left behind a wonderful program to build on, will make a call on his staff in the future, but said those who "live and breathe" for the jersey will be at the top of his list.

He played most of his career under his lifelong mentor Wayne Bennett, who has said he would assist the new coach where he can.

"He is the supercoach. I would be silly not to get his advice on things," Boyd said when asked if Bennett would be on his team.

Meninga, who coached Boyd in the glory years, also shaped the way he will approach the task.

Boyd said that "the history and what it meant to play for Queensland and how Origin started and the legacy those guys left behind" was a key message of Meninga that got the best out of the Maroons.

"It is a challenging job to be out in the cauldron and play at the highest level and perform at your best," Boyd said.

"Mal was really good at getting the best out of you emotionally and mentally and making sure you were prepared come game night."

QRL chairman Brian Canavan said once Slater stepped down after winning three of five series, the organisation came up with a list of candidates and Boyd was the standout.

"If you go back five years ago Billy was at the same point," he said.

"He hadn't had the formal NRL coaching experience. Darius has more experience than Billy had back then. That gave us confidence to go to a new phase.

"Billy has left the place and program in great shape, and Darius will step in and put his own spin on things.":

Bennett was a great support on and off the field to Boyd and will be there to lean on.

"The advice Wayne offered was that he would support whoever we appointed, and Wayne has had a long association with Darius and knows his great strengths," Canavan said.

"The most important thing for this job is the identity with the state.

"What he has got is the pride and passion for the jersey and the state and this connection with players and appetite for the historical aspects of the jersey and embedding it in players."

Boyd entered a mental health facility at a key moment in his NRL career and has since been a leader in that space.

It was a turning point and he now understands the mental side of life and footy.

"It has been a journey for me on and off the field. It is a great opportunity for me to instil belief, confidence and desire into the next generation," he said.

stories.headline: MLB trade deadline 2026: Winners and losers, one month later
stories.summary: Here's how all 30 teams have scored -- or struck out -- so far.
stories.body:
Today marks the one-month anniversary of a frenetic 2026 MLB trade deadline. What, if anything, has changed since then?

At the time, we did a lot of quick-turn analysis and rating of each move, as well as the deadline as a whole. But none of that was meant to be the final word. It was our best attempt at an initial assessment based on the information we had at the time, while considering the landscape as it stood in MLB when the deadline hit. In reality, it will take years to fully untangle many of the moves made last month. That's just the time scale of baseball.

One month later, we still can't make any final proclamations about those moves. The samples are just too small. What we can do is take a fresh look at all that movement by asking a simple question about every team: How has it worked out so far?

In reconsidering the deadline one month hence, we'll keep our focus on the postseason races and not so much the prospects who changed teams, players whose destinies are a long way from being determined. The playoff chase is something different: On the morning of Nov. 1, if not sooner, we'll know everything we need to know about that.

To sift through the deadline fallout, I developed a rating to sort the teams based on how their fortunes evolved and how their deadline acquisitions have performed. I've also grouped them into tiers, based on how things have gone.

Tier 1: Contenders whose deadline pickups have helped and whose playoff odds have improved

Atlanta Braves (Post-deadline rating: 108.6)
Playoff% change: +0.3% | Pickup impact: 10.9

The Braves' deadline would stand out if the only move made by Alex Anthopoulos was to acquire starter Tyler Mahle from the Giants. That's how good Mahle has been, posting a 1.48 ERA over five starts and rolling up 1.4 bWAR in his first month as a Brave. It's not really out of nowhere. He has been a very good pitcher for a long time, including last season when he posted a 2.18 ERA in 16 starts for Texas. But he was just 3-9 with a 5.13 ERA for San Francisco before the trade. He allowed five runs in his last start for the Giants -- the same number of runs he gave up in his first five starts for the Braves.

Meanwhile, high-energy lefty Brent Suter has been a strong addition to the bullpen. Lane Thomas, the primary addition to the lineup, has struggled, but in terms of a short, quick and much-needed impact, Mahle has thus far been the best pickup of the deadline. As a club, the Braves have been status quo -- which in most instances would be sufficient, but in the Braves' case, they're dealing with a white-hot Phillies team running them down in the division race.

Toronto Blue Jays (108.4)
Playoff% change: +8.6% | Pickup impact: 1.1

The Blue Jays were on the fence at the deadline, not tearing down by any stretch but keeping the focus on the longer term at the same time. Daulton Varsho and Kevin Gausman were traded, but Gausman was immediately replaced by ex-Angel Jose Soriano in the rotation. Former Cubs prospect Brett Bateman was part of the return for Gausman, and while that was a big-picture move, he was added to the big league roster and so far has played well as an on-base speed guy at the plate and impact defender.

The Blue Jays have won just enough to remain on the fringe of the American League wild-card cluster, an outcome that justifies their on-the-fence deadline approach.

Tampa Bay Rays (108.3)
Playoff% change: +0.3% | Pickup impact: 3.3

The Rays were winning an average of 94 games in the sims at the time of the deadline; that number has since reached 96.1, the sixth-biggest uptick in the majors. Meanwhile, the Rays rank fifth in player impact from their acquisitions. In other words, so far so good for Tampa Bay's deadline performance. This rating doesn't even include the apparent end of the Rays' interminable quest for a new ballpark.

As for those acquisitions, Freddy Peralta has made only two quality outings out of five, but Liam Hicks has hit like Johnny Bench behind the plate, and Tyler Wells has been a standout in the bullpen. If Peralta can build on his promising last start -- six shutout innings in Detroit -- this outlook only gets better.

Chicago Cubs (104.8)
Playoff% change: +3.2% | Pickup impact: 6.2

The Cubs are second behind Atlanta in deadline player impact, but despite an epic month from their power hitters, Chicago's win projection hasn't changed much. The Cubs' pitching hasn't quite kept pace with their hot hitting, though both trajectories have been impacted by the weather at Wrigley Field. Clay Holmes has been fantastic, stabilizing the rotation. The same mostly holds true for Gausman, though the veteran righty has mixed in a couple of so-so outings with three good ones.

Other pickups have had surprising impacts. Outfielder Tyrone Taylor has a 1.027 OPS for his first 19 games for the Cubs, and Aaron Civale's 1.54 ERA in a multi-inning relief role lessens the disappointment over Ryan Zeferjahn's early struggles in Chicago.

Los Angeles Dodgers (103.4)
Playoff% change: 0.0% | Pickup impact: 6.2

Technically, the Dodgers' postseason odds didn't go up -- but that's just because there was nowhere else to go: L.A. was at 100% then, and remains so now.

The Dodgers' deadline at this point comes down to Tarik Skubal, who has pitched true to form but hasn't gotten a lot of support. His ERA over five starts (3.00) along with his lone win doesn't reflect how well he has pitched, as evidenced by his 2.28 FIP.

The Dodgers have been so-so as a team over this span, which for them is enough to spur plenty of hand-wringing about their ability to pull off a three-peat. All we can say at the moment is that whatever L.A.'s struggles might be, they're not Skubal's fault.

Tier 2: Contenders whose deadline pickups haven't helped, but whose playoff odds have improved anyway

Baltimore Orioles (103.2)
Playoff% change: +10.6% | Pickup impact: -0.9

It's not surprising that the Orioles have a negative pickup impact because they were very much in subtract mode at the deadline. Despite that, Baltimore has played its best sustained baseball all season over the last month, even crawling back to the .500 mark.

Things have gone so well that the Orioles went into late-stage add mode, claiming ex-Met Luis Robert Jr. off waivers just before the cutoff for postseason eligibility. With Pete Alonso leading the way, the Orioles still have a shot at taking advantage of that eligibility. It's an excellent example of how a team's deadline behavior doesn't always correlate to how it plays afterward.

Philadelphia Phillies (100.5)
Playoff% change: +34.2% | Pickup impact: -6.9

The Phillies have gone 19-7 since the deadline and improved their win projection in the simulations by more than five wins, easily the biggest uptick of the contending teams. Hard to complain about that.

At the same time, their deadline activity isn't necessarily directly connected to their results. Luis Arraez has felt like a perfect fit for the Phillies' lineup, but his actual output so far (.704 OPS) has been modest. Brooks Raley has been fine in the bullpen. Both might still play key roles for a team that has high October aspirations, but so far, the Phillies have been on a roll for other reasons.

Texas Rangers (98.8)
Playoff% change: +13.5% | Pickup impact: -2.4

The Rangers are another AL club that has continued to muddle around the .500 mark, but that's enough, given their division and league, to keep their playoff probabilities trending in the right direction. It's like treading water even as the tide pushes you closer to shore.

Texas had a quiet deadline as a fence-rider, and it hasn't gotten much from primary pickups Adam Macko, Chase Silseth and Logan O'Hoppe. The Rangers have continued to work the ends of their roster with depth moves that don't fall under the umbrella of deadline activity, so it's not like Chris Young and his staff are just sitting on their hands. But the Rangers were on the fence a month ago and would remain so today if the deadline were a month later. Texas remains a hard team to read.

Cleveland Guardians (98.6)
Playoff% change: +14.3% | Pickup impact: -1.2

Jo Adell has been just what the Guardians needed, while doing the same things he was doing for the Angels. He has been one of the more impactful deadline pickups so far.

Cleveland as a whole has continued hovering around .500 over the last month. Likewise, the Guardians' additions other than Adell have been mixed. Nathaniel Lowe has had a couple of nice moments, but overall has a 92 OPS+. Foster Griffin has been solid after a rough first start after arriving from Washington. Craig Yoho has gotten frequent relief work, but the ex-Brewer has an ERA over 7.00.

San Diego Padres (97.9)
Playoff% change: +29.6% | Pickup impact: -5.5

Despite flagging playoff odds and a roster that seemed to be going stale, A.J. Preller orchestrated an aggressive deadline approach, as he is wont to do, adding Robbie Ray and Casey Mize to the rotation. Ray has been in full-blown Robbie Ray mode since arriving in San Diego, filling up the walks column and yet often managing to successfully traverse the highwire. Mize has been all over the place from really good to really not, but overall his Padre ERA is well over 6.00.

Other pickups haven't played much. So the early returns haven't been great for the acquisitions and yet the Padres rank fifth in post-deadline run differential and have solidified their playoff odds. They need that momentum to continue and, for that, they figure to need more consistency from their deadline adds.

Milwaukee Brewers (97.6)
Playoff% change: +0.1% | Pickup impact: -5.3

Most of Milwaukee's pickups so far have proved to be organizational depth. Of those who have played much of a role with the big league club, Dustin May has fallen off after two good starts upon being sprinkled with the Brewers' magic pixie dust, and Antonio Senzatela hasn't been able to work himself into a high-leverage role.

The good news: The Brewers just keep rolling and look like a good bet to repeat as the National League's top seed.

New York Yankees (96.2)
Playoff% change: +1.6% | Pickup impact: -5.9

The Yankees' play has ticked up since the deadline. It's not because of Brian Cashman's pickups, in total. Heliot Ramos has hit .148 and managed to get a half-win below replacement in just a month as a Yankee. His rough start has been offset by solid hitting from Luis Garcia Jr. (0.6 bWAR, 133 OPS+). It's a wash between New York's two deadline additions.

Nothing much has changed for the Yankees. All season goals remain on the table and the chances of reaching them might be determined by when Aaron Judge is back and how quickly he can return to form.

Boston Red Sox (93.4)
Playoff% change: +4.0% | Pickup impact: -4.2

The Red Sox have been just over .500 since the deadline, good enough to nudge their playoff odds in the right direction even though the run prevention has been lackluster during that stretch. Only five teams have given up more post-deadline runs. Surprising addition Erik Miller has been dynamite as a bullpen lefty, so the negative impact isn't on him. But Curtis Mead was injured in his first game for Boston and Adley Rutschman hasn't hit. None of this has impeded Boston's progress, and it would be unsurprising if the second month for the pickups proves to be better than the first.

We should note that if you want to count Jahmai Jones as a deadline pickup, which we don't because it was a mid-July, DFA-related move, the player impact number would be better. Jones has been off the charts in his role as a lefty-mashing righty bat off the bench, hitting .481/.600/1.037 in 35 plate appearances against southpaws since joining Boston.

Chicago White Sox (93.1)
Playoff% change: +20.1% | Pickup impact: -7.2

The White Sox have played better than .500 ball for weeks now, good enough to expand their edge in the AL Central race and keep them out in front of the key chase for the circuit's No. 2 playoff seed.

If Chris Getz's deadline pickups had done more, the White Sox might already be counting down their AL Central magic number. Joey Bart was injured, preventing him from filling Chicago's hole behind the plate. Luis Castillo has been even worse for the White Sox than he was for the Mariners, and that's saying something. Huascar Brazoban not only didn't emerge as a high-leverage option before going on the injured list, he didn't look like a big league reliever, posting a 6.30 ERA with a 6.49 FIP. Brenton Doyle's inability to add much at the plate perhaps contributed to Getz's late-month pivot to acquire Tommy Pham and Jake Cave. All of these things can improve, and for the White Sox to finish off their amazing Cinderella push, they probably should.

Tier 3: Contender whose pickups have helped, but whose playoff odds have dropped

Arizona Diamondbacks (98.4)
Playoff% change: -30.2% | Pickup impact: 1.1

Arizona has played losing baseball since the deadline, both in the win-loss columns and in terms of run differential. So even though the Diamondbacks remain neck and neck with the Padres in the push for the NL's last playoff slot, the simulations have started to prefer the hot Padres.

The downturn in Arizona's playoff chances is an almost exact match for San Diego's uptick. Arizona made only one deadline move, adding Lars Nootbaar from St. Louis. Nootbaar has played solid ball, enjoying a couple of big moments that have paid off in the win probability component of AXE while getting on base consistently. Still, if the Diamondbacks fall short of the playoff bracket, Mike Hazen's passive deadline might deserve some scrutiny.

Tier 4: Contender whose pickups haven't helped and whose playoff odds have dropped

Houston Astros (95.2)
Playoff% change: -0.8% | Pickup impact: -1.6

The Astros haven't played well since the deadline, and their one significant addition, center fielder Daulton Varsho, has hit so poorly he hasn't come close to making up for it with his plus defense. Houston has outplayed its post-deadline run differential by a couple of games or this would look even worse.

The Astros were in an add position and would remain so, but that's not because their roster is close to complete. It's just how the AL West landscape shapes up. Maybe the roster had too many holes to address at the deadline, but you could argue that if the Astros were going to make only one deadline splash, maybe they should have addressed their rotation.

Tier 5: Teams all but out of contention

Minnesota Twins (101.4)

Pittsburgh Pirates (101.4)

St. Louis Cardinals (99.3)

Miami Marlins (98.9)

Detroit Tigers (89.0)

Seattle Mariners (86.8)

All of these clubs were fence-sitters at the deadline, or at least were flagged as such by their playoff chances. Despite that, the Twins and Pirates added on deadline day, and while the contributions from the pickups of both teams have been encouraging, it hasn't prevented a bleeding of playoff odds. Together, the Twins and Pirates have gone 22-29 despite the production of additions like A.J. Minter and Dean Kremer (Twins) and Camilo Doval and Kirby Yates (Pirates). At least they tried.

The Cardinals and Marlins both subtracted at the deadline and have gone on much as they did before, remaining on the outer perimeter of wild-card contention, which is better than a collapse but none too inspiring. The Tigers and Mariners, on the other hand, have collapsed one year after they faced each other in the division series.

Tier 6: Non-contenders

Kansas City Royals (111.0)

New York Mets (108.9)

Colorado Rockies (100.2)

Cincinnati Reds (99.9)

Washington Nationals (98.2)

San Francisco Giants (96.8)

Athletics (93.3)

Los Angeles Angels (90.7)

All of these teams appropriately subtracted at the deadline, though the Royals were fairly passive in doing so. Still, they, along with the Mets, have played much better baseball since the deadline, reminding their fans of why they had high hopes when the season began. Of course, that kind of thing can exacerbate the frustrations of a fanbase wondering where these wins were a few months ago. Of the two, the Mets are in more of an overall reshuffling than the Royals, a process that will be aided by what was baseball's largest haul of prospects during the deadline period.

The Royals, on the other hand, have looked like the offensive team we thought they could be as their lineup has gotten healthier. That has paid off in wins because the completely made-over bullpen has been much more reliable, even as it's built on the work of recycled veterans like Nate Pearson and future Hall of Famer Craig Kimbrel. It's a key lesson: If a bullpen mix isn't working, shake it up sooner rather than later because so much of bullpen management is a constant catching of lightning in a bottle.
